title: Dialogue and refutation beat exposition
statement: Where there is time, explain through a dialogue that answers a learner's questions, or by refuting the wrong idea, rather than by straight exposition.
example: In one study of 364 students, a dialogue version beat straight exposition by an effect size of 0.83 and a refutation version by 0.79.
detail: An intro-video BrainLift for a Grade 3 reading course reports Muller, Bewes, Sharma and Reimann (2008): 364 students met the same physics content in four formats, a dialogue version beat straight exposition at d = 0.83 and a refutation version at d = 0.79, and the lowest-prior-knowledge students gained most (`downloads/BrainLift - What makes a good intro video.md`, line 471). The same document calls two voices, one asking as a learner and one answering, the gold standard for its videos (lines 303 to 305). The source names the study without a link; its DOI was found on Crossref.
against: For media under a minute the same document prefers a single voice, since a dialogue needs three turns for one idea and is too rushed below about 60 seconds (`downloads/BrainLift - What makes a good intro video.md`, lines 307 and 426).
